title: Nand Lal's kitchen
hook: tradition says the Guru praised Nand Lal's langar above others because it served everyone, anytime

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rehat words: writings on how a Sikh should live, with Nand Lal asking and the Guru answering. Your line was a rule kept. Today, the same poet, in his kitchen.

The dinner rush is over. Chairs are up on the tables, the floor is wet, the cook is wiping down the last pan. A traveler knocks on the glass. Kitchen's closed, someone mouths, pointing at the sign with the hours. Nobody is being cruel. Hours are hours. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a kitchen with no such sign. It belonged to the Persian poet we met a few days ago, the one who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court. Today: langar.
screen: `THE CHAIRS ARE UP ON THE TABLES.` → `KITCHEN'S CLOSED.` → `A KITCHEN WITH NO SIGN.`

segments.voice: This story comes to us as a sakhi, a story passed on, not from Nand Lal's own poems. At Anandpur, tradition says, several Sikhs ran langars, free kitchens. The Guru wanted to see what they were really like, so he went round them dressed as an ordinary traveler, at an hour when no meal was being served. At one door he was told to come back later. At another, the food wasn't ready, so there was nothing to give. Then he came to Nand Lal's kitchen, and whatever was in the pots, finished or not, was put in front of him straight away. Later, the story goes, the Guru praised Nand Lal's langar above the others. Not because the food was finer. Because it served everyone, anytime. A few things are folded into that. Hunger doesn't keep office hours: someone who arrives late is exactly as hungry as someone who arrives on time. The other kitchens weren't wicked; they were organized. The story isn't against good planning, only against the plan becoming a reason to send someone away. Nand Lal didn't wait for the meal to be perfect. He gave what there was, as it was. And notice who the traveler turned out to be. In Sikh telling, the one you serve at the odd hour may be the Guru himself, so the langar never needs to check. A gurdwara langar keeps the same idea today: food for whoever walks in, without asking who they are.
screen: `THE GURU GOES ROUND IN DISGUISE.` · `COME BACK LATER. NOTHING READY.` · `NAND LAL SERVES WHAT THERE IS.` · `HUNGER KEEPS NO OFFICE HOURS.` · then, large: `SERVE ANYTIME.`

segments.voice: Picture who might turn up hungry outside the usual hours, a roommate coming in late, a coworker who skipped lunch, a delivery driver, and choose one. Then choose what you already have, fruit, tea, leftovers, as they are, and picture handing it over without asking anything first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture it.
Langar, the free kitchen that, in the story, fed a stranger at the wrong hour with whatever was in the pots, and was praised for it.
Your line: serve anytime. Hunger keeps no office hours, and neither did his kitchen. See you tomorrow.
